title: Case-Control vs Cohort Study: Key Differences | AnswerThis
summary: Cohort studies follow people from exposure to outcome. Case-control studies start from the outcome and look back. See when to use each.
body_markdown:
A cohort study starts from the exposure and follows people forward to see who develops the outcome. A case-control study starts from the outcome and looks back to compare past exposure in people with and without it.


This guide compares the two designs side by side. It explains each one with an example, shows what each can measure and helps you choose the right design for your question.


## TL;DR


-


A cohort study moves from exposure to outcome. A case-control study moves from outcome back to exposure.


-


A cohort study can measure incidence and the risk ratio. A case-control study gives the odds ratio.


-


Use a case-control study for a rare disease. Use a cohort study for a rare exposure.


-


Both are observational designs, so both need a plan for confounding.


-


Report either design with STROBE, and appraise it with a tool such as the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.


## Case-control vs cohort study: what is the difference?


Feature


Cohort study


Case-control study


Starting point


People grouped by exposure


People grouped by outcome: cases and controls


Direction in time


Forward, from exposure to outcome


Backward, from outcome to past exposure


What it measures


Incidence, risk ratio and rate ratio


Odds ratio. It does not measure incidence.


Cost and time


Often high. Follow-up can take years.


Lower. There is no follow-up period.


Rare diseases


Inefficient. You need a very large group to see enough cases.


Efficient. You begin with the cases.


Rare exposures


Efficient. You can recruit exposed people on purpose.


Inefficient. Few cases or controls will have the exposure.


Main biases


Loss to follow-up and confounding


Recall bias, poor choice of controls and confounding


## What is a cohort study?


A cohort study selects people who do not have the outcome yet. It records who is exposed and who is not. It then compares how many people in each group develop the outcome.


### Prospective and retrospective cohort studies


-


Prospective. You recruit people now and follow them into the future.


-


Retrospective. You use existing records. The exposure and the outcome have already happened, but you still start from the exposure and move forward through the records.


### Cohort study example


Researchers recruit 2,000 nurses who have no heart disease. Half work night shifts and half work day shifts. The researchers follow both groups for ten years and compare how many nurses in each group develop heart disease. This example is invented for this guide.


## What is a case-control study?


A case-control study selects people by outcome. It then compares how common a past exposure was in each group.


### Cases and controls


Cases are people who have the disease. Controls are people who do not have it. Controls should come from the same population that produced the cases.


### Matching


Researchers often match each case with one or more controls of the same age and sex. Matching makes the two groups alike on those factors.


### Nested case-control study


In a nested case-control study, the cases and controls both come from inside an existing cohort. Exposure data were collected before the disease, which reduces recall bias.


### Case-control study example


Researchers identify 200 patients with a rare cancer and 400 patients without it from the same hospitals. They ask both groups about past pesticide exposure and compare the odds of exposure. This example is invented for this guide.


## Risk ratio vs odds ratio


Both measures come from a 2 × 2 table of exposure and disease.


-


The risk ratio compares the risk of disease in exposed and unexposed people. You need a cohort study to calculate it.


-


The odds ratio compares the odds. It is the measure a case-control study gives, because the researcher decides how many cases and controls to include.


### When is the odds ratio close to the risk ratio?


The two are close only when the outcome is rare. Explore the[guide](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6213310/) as an outcome in less than 10 percent of the study population. Two worked examples show why.


Rare outcome. Of 1,000 exposed people, 30 develop the disease. Of 1,000 unexposed people, 10 develop it.


-


Risk ratio = (30 ÷ 1,000) ÷ (10 ÷ 1,000) = 3.00


-


Odds ratio = (30 × 990) ÷ (970 × 10) = 3.06


Common outcome. Of 100 exposed people, 60 develop the disease. Of 100 unexposed people, 30 develop it.


-


Risk ratio = (60 ÷ 100) ÷ (30 ÷ 100) = 2.00


-


Odds ratio = (60 × 70) ÷ (40 × 30) = 3.50


Outcome


Risk ratio


Odds ratio


Rare: 2 percent of people


3.00


3.06


Common: 45 percent of people


2.00


3.50


When the outcome is common, the odds ratio is further from 1 than the risk ratio. Do not report it as if it were a risk ratio.


The AnswerThis[effect size calculator](https://answerthis.io/effect-size-calculator) is free and has no limit on runs. It computes odds ratios with intervals from a labelled 2 × 2 table. Keep in mind that an odds ratio is not a risk ratio.


## A famous example: smoking and lung cancer


The two designs often work together. The research on smoking and lung cancer is the best-known case, and[an article](https://www.nature.com/articles/milecancer08) tells the story.


1.


In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill reported a case-control study in the British Medical Journal. They concluded that smoking was “a cause, and an important cause” of lung cancer.


2.


To answer concerns about bias, they then designed a prospective cohort study of British doctors.


3.


The first report of the cohort study appeared in 1954. It confirmed the case-control findings.


The case-control study gave an early answer. The cohort study then tested that answer with a stronger design.


## How do you choose between them?


-


Choose a case-control study when the disease is rare, when you want to test several exposures for one disease, or when time and budget are limited.


-


Choose a cohort study when the exposure is rare, when you want to study several outcomes of one exposure, or when you need incidence or a risk ratio.


-


Consider a retrospective cohort study when good records already exist. It gives cohort measures without a long wait.


## How do you report and appraise these studies?


### Reporting: STROBE


The[STROBE Statement](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17941714/) is a checklist of 22 items for reports of observational studies. Eighteen items apply to cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies alike. Four items are specific to the design. Its explanation and elaboration paper gives an example for each item ([Vandenbroucke et al., 2007](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0040297) ).


STROBE tells you what to report. It is not a tool for judging the quality of a study.


### Appraisal: the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale


The[Newcastle-Ottawa Scale](https://ohri.ca/sites/ohri/files/2025-09/nosgen.pdf) has one form for cohort studies and one for case-control studies. Each form gives stars in three areas: selection, comparability, and outcome or exposure. A study can earn up to nine stars.


The AnswerThis[risk of bias assessment tool](https://answerthis.io/risk-of-bias) assesses one study at a time. It gives draft answers linked to evidence from the paper, and it includes the Newcastle-Ottawa cohort and case-control forms. The first study is free. A reviewer must confirm each answer.


## Check your reporting before you submit


The AnswerThis[STROBE checklist checker](https://answerthis.io/strobe-checklist) reviews the reporting in your manuscript against STROBE 2007 for a cohort, case-control or cross-sectional study. Choose your study design and paste your text, or select Load example to see how it works. One manuscript is free. STROBE is a reporting guideline and not a quality-assessment instrument, so use an appraisal tool to judge study quality.


## FAQs


### Which design gives stronger evidence?


A cohort study usually gives stronger evidence, because the exposure is recorded before the outcome. For a rare disease, a well-run case-control study is the practical choice.


### Is a case-control study always retrospective?


It always looks back at past exposure. The cases themselves can be recruited as new diagnoses occur.


### Can a cohort study be retrospective?


Yes. A retrospective cohort study uses existing records, but it still moves from exposure to outcome.


### Why can a case-control study not measure risk?


The researcher decides how many cases and controls to include. The share of people with the disease in the study is set by design, so it does not show the true risk.


### Are case-control and cohort studies both observational?


Yes. In both, the researcher observes exposure and does not assign it.


### What is a nested case-control study?


It is a case-control study carried out inside an existing cohort. The cases and the controls both come from that cohort.
